newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Izetbegovic seeks probe into alleged corruption.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic seeks probe into alleged corruption.

text.p: The Moslem chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, said on Monday he planned to form a special commission to investigate possible government corruption.
Izetbegovic said the special commission would include international representatives and would investigate the use of peacetime aid donated to Bosnia.
"If accusations of corruption prove to be based on facts, the responsible persons will be arrested and brought to court without delay," Izetbegovic said in a statement read to reporters.

Allegations of corruption have emerged as an explosive post-war issue since the president of Bosnia's Serb entity, Biljana Plavsic, accused her government rivals last month of running smuggling rackets.
Plavsic's allegations also implicated officials in the Moslem-Croat federation, which together with the Serb republic comprises the post-war state of Bosnia.

Izetbegovic said his decision was prompted by comments by British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook who was quoted in a London newspaper over the weekend saying aid funds had been misused by Bosnian authorities.
"We are deeply concerned that sums of money we have put into Bosnia have not been used for the purposes intended," Cook was quoted as saying by The Sunday Times.
The newspaper, citing unnamed sources, alleged that Moslem authorities had abused "transition assistance credit" funds donated last year by the World Bank earmarked for supporting the state budget.
Izetbegovic said he would request Cook's assistance when they met on Tuesday during the foreign secretary's visit to Bosnia.
Western officials and Croat and Serb leaders have raised questions about the expenditure of a portion of the $120 million transition assistance credit (TAC).
Up to $15 million of the funds were channelled to Moslem municipalities and state enterprises by Moslem authorities under the Moslem-led caretaker government, Western officials say.
World Bank officials say they would have preferred the money be spent for more pressing financial needs but say no law was broken.
Izetbegovic looked angry as he read out his statement and declined to answer questions afterward.
He said if the allegations of corruption proved false, he would ask that foreigners "spreading such lies" leave the country without delay.

"They (some foreign enemies) are waging some kind of special personal war against the Bosnian leadership in order to prove their thesis that there was no aggression here, that it was a civil war and that all (warring) sides are the same," he said.
Bosnian opposition parties repeated calls on Monday for a full accounting of possible corruption and alleged abuse of reconstruction aid.

In a statement issued in Sarajevo, the shadow cabinet "requests that the international community conducts an energetic and independent investigation of these allegations" and suggested United Nations police monitors participate.

The independent Sarajevo weekly Slobodna Bosna alleged this month that Moslem authorities in the northwest Bihac region were enriching themselves by embezzling equipment from state companies and avoiding customs taxes.
